For this purpose, low altitude platforms such as drones have great potential to provide high resolution optical imagery where Machine Learning (ML) applied to classify different types of crops. In this research work, crop classification is performed at different phenological stages using optical images which are obtained from drone. For this purpose, gray level co-occurrence matrix (GLCM) based features are extracted from underlying gray scale images collected by the drone. To classify the different types of crops, different ML algorithms including Random Forest (RF), Naive Bayes (NB), Neural Network (NN) and Support Vector Machine (SVM) are applied. The results showed that the ML algorithms performed much better on GLCM features as compared to gray scale images with a margin of 13.65% in overall accuracy. Keywords: Machine learning, Remote sensing, Texture analysis, Classification, Unmanned aerial vehicles, Feature extraction, GLCM Introduction Remote sensing is a valuable tool in evaluating, monitoring, and management of land, water, and crop resources. Satellite imagery and aerial imagery have wide applications in the field of agriculture, monitoring snow cover trends, wildfire trends, water level rising, and forestry. In agriculture, crop health monitoring, yield estimation, classification of crops based on land cover, and monitoring of droughts are some common applications of remote sensing (Navalgund, Jayaraman & Roy, 2007; Seelan et al., 2003; Hufkens et al., 2019; Sivakumar et al., 2004). Among these applications, crop classification is quite challenging due to the texture and color similarity of crops in the initial stages. For this purpose, satellite data is commonly used which provides free access to the data. The data obtained from such platforms is coarse in a resolution which makes it difficult to classify the different types of crops. Apart from a coarse resolution of satellite data, the effect of atmospheric particles and cloud cover percentage in the image, if greater than 90% will result in discarding the images as no valuable information can be extracted from the satellite for these images. The low-cost Un-manned Aerial Vehicles (UAV) are the substitute of the satellite platforms which provide high-resolution data with flexibility in data collection. After high-resolution images acquisition, several Machine/Deep Learning (ML/DL) algorithms are applied to classify the different types of crops. A lot of applications use texture information as features that are further given as input to the ML classification algorithms. The texture features provide useful insights into the color, its spatial arrangement, and intensities. In Kwak & Park (2019), the crop classification based on texture features is performed on the data collected by a drone mounted with a multi-spectral camera. The acquired images are up-scaled to 25 cm resolution and mosaiced later to obtain a complete field of view. To extract texture features, Gray Level Co-occurrence Matrix (GLCM) at different kernel sizes is used including 3 × 3, 15 × 15, and 31 × 31. The mosaiced images act as an input to classification algorithms, such as Random Forest and Support Vector Machine (SVM). It is seen that using textural features obtained from larger kernel size showed improvement in classification results by 7.72% in overall accuracy rather than only using spectral information for classification. Similarly in Böhler, Schaepman & Kneubühler (2018), texture base classification of crops is performed at pixel and parcel-based level where the crops in the study are maize, bare soil, sugar beat, winter wheat, and grassland. The images are acquired by eBee UAV in four flights of 30 min each on 26 June 2015. Textural features are extracted from the obtained UAV images. Random forest algorithm is applied after extracting the texture features which obtained an overall accuracy of 86.3%. In this study, we performed a classification of four different types of crops including wheat, soybean, rice, maize. The main objective of this research is to investigate the texture feature-based crop classification of different crops having the same spatial texture and colors. The high-resolution optical images are acquired by the drone. The multiple texture features are extracted including contrast, homogeneity, dimensionality, angular second moment, energy, and correlation. To perform classification, Support Vector Machine, Naive Bayes, Random Forest, and Neural Network are applied on the grayscale images and the texture features. fetched_contents.text: A comparison of pixel-based and object-based image analysis with selected machine learning algorithms for the classification of agricultural landscapes using SPOT-5 HRG imagery Abstract Pixel-based and object-based image analysis approaches for classifying broad land cover classes over agricultural landscapes are compared using three supervised machine learning algorithms: decision tree (DT), random forest (RF), and the support vector machine (SVM). Overall classification accuracies between pixel-based and object-based classifications were not statistically significant (p > 0.05) when the same machine learning algorithms were applied. Using object-based image analysis, there was a statistically significant difference in classification accuracy between maps produced using the DT algorithm compared to maps produced using either RF (p = 0.0116) or SVM algorithms (p = 0.0067). Using pixel-based image analysis, there was no statistically significant difference (p > 0.05) between results produced using different classification algorithms. Classifications based on RF and SVM algorithms provided a more visually adequate depiction of wetland, riparian, and crop land cover types when compared to DT based classifications, using either object-based or pixel-based image analysis. In this study, pixel-based classifications utilized fewer variables (15 vs. 300), achieved similar classification accuracies, and required less time to produce than object-based classifications. Object-based classifications produced a visually appealing generalized appearance of land cover classes. Based exclusively on overall accuracy reports, there was no advantage to preferring one image analysis approach over another for the purposes of mapping broad land cover types in agricultural environments using medium spatial resolution earth observation imagery. Highlights ► Pixel-based (PB) and object-based (OB) classifications are compared. ► Three machine learning algorithms (MLAs) are examined. ► No statistical difference between PB and OB classifications was found. ► For OB classifications, significant differences between MLAs were found. Keywords Comparison ; Object-based ; Decision tree ; Random forest ; Support vector machine Introduction The classification of land use and land cover (LULC) from remotely sensed imagery can be divided into two general image analysis approaches: i) classifications based on pixels, and ii) classifications based on objects. While pixel-based analysis has long been the mainstay approach for classifying remotely sensed imagery, object-based image analysis has become increasingly commonplace over the last decade (Blaschke, 2010). Whether pixels or objects are used as underlying units for the purposes of classifying remotely derived imagery, the information contained within - and among - these units (e.g., spectral, textural, etc.) can be subjected to a variety of classification algorithms. Previous comparative studies have been conducted that examine the relative performance of different classification algorithms using pixel-based, and/or object-based image analysis. A brief summary of selected comparisons is provided below. Using pixel-based based image analysis on Landsat Thematic Mapper (TM) data, Huang et al. (2002) compared thematic mapping accuracies produced using four different classification algorithms: support vector machines (SVMs), decision trees (DTs), a neural network classifier, and the maximum likelihood classifier (MLC). Their results suggested that the accuracy of SVM-based classifications generally outperformed the other three classification algorithms. Pal (2005) compared the accuracies of two supervised classification algorithms using Landsat Enhanced Thematic Mapper (ETM +) data: SVMs and Random Forests (RFs) (Breiman, 2001), and found that they performed equally well. Gislason et al. (2006) compared a RF approach to a variety of decision tree-like algorithms using pixel-based image analysis of Landsat MSS data. They found that the selected tree-like algorithms tested performed similarly, but that the RF algorithm outperformed the standard implementation of Breiman et al.'s (1984) DTs; however, their findings also showed that the RF algorithm performed slightly less well than a modified DT algorithm (boosted 1R). Carreiras et al. (2006) examined several classification algorithms, which included standard DTs, quadratic discriminant analysis, probability-bagging classification trees (PBCT), and k-nearest neighbors (K-NN) using pixel-based analysis of spatially coarse (1 km pixels) SPOT-4 VEGETATION imagery. Their results, verified by 10-fold cross-validation, showed that the PBCT algorithm produced the best overall classification accuracy. Brenning (2009) compared eleven classification algorithms using a pixel-based image analysis, and Landsat ETM + imagery, for the detection of rock glaciers. Using Landsat TM and ETM + data, Otukei and Blaschke (2010) compared the MLC, SVM, and DT algorithms in a pixel-based approach, and found DTs performed better than MLC and SVM. fetched_contents.text: Land use and land cover (LULC) performance modeling using machine learning algorithms: a case study of the city of Melbourne, Australia Introduction Land Use and Land Cover (LULC) information derived from remote sensing images is widely used for the aggregation of spatial information, e.g., for the preparation of maps. Firstly, due to the public availability of remote sensing images. Secondly, the analytical capabilities with add-on machine learning algorithms in the public domain. The maps serve as the foundational spatial layer in smart city planning, environmental management, sustainable development, and resilient infrastructure design. The extraction of LULC information is governed by their similarities and dissimilarities in spectral, textural, geometric, and contextual properties stacked in the images. However, the dissection of such properties in an objective and automated manner assists in extracting precise LULC information. Due to the wide application of LULC information and derived maps in smart city planning, their quality needs to be assessed. In LULC classification, deep learning (DL)-based methods in recent studies1,2,3 have resulted in significant performance improvements. Nevertheless, these methods are not only ineffective/inefficient on limited datasets but also have limited interpretability and explainability. Therefore, the use of non-deep learning-based methods4,5, which leverage handcrafted geospatial information such as spectral and statistical-based features for the classification, has been preferred to deal with these limitations. The quality of LULC maps derived from remote sensing images can be characterised using spectral, statistical, and indices-based features. These features and their various combinations can further be assessed in an automated way using state-of-the-art machine learning (ML) algorithms, thus providing quality assurance of the derived products. The performance of employed ML algorithms provides the reliability and assurance of the LULC maps for their use in smart city planning, among many other applications. Thus, derived reliable maps can further be used for balanced sustainable city development and mapping of the coverage of urban green space6,7. Despite the usefulness of LULC maps in sustainable development, accurate and precise delineation and detection of LULC in urban settings from remotely sensed images is challenging due to dense physical arrangements and composition of the features, proximity to infrastructure, and complex distribution of assets in multiple hierarchies. Therefore, precise characterisation of the spatial, spectral, and statistical properties of images using understandable and applicable algorithms and deriving accurate LULC is an open challenge for the spatial information and planning research community. However, with the advancement of ML algorithms, there are potential capabilities that need convergence for a replicable, interpretable, and explainable approach. To contribute to overcoming the existing problems and tackling the challenges, we focus in this study on three key features namely: statistical pattern of reflectance under different bands, spectral information, and leveraging the spectral indices (which are calculated using different spectral bands). Real-world features in images primarily inherit three complementary sources of information (statistical, spectral, and indices-based) which characterise the objects in different dimensions. Characterising this information by dissecting their interrelationships and revealing the redundancy associated with them improves the separability and delineation of the frontiers of LULC classes. Thus, guiding and helping smart city planning practitioners and researchers. This article’s main contributions are four-fold: 1. (1) We design seven different schemes of characterisation of LULC and classify them with five traditional ML algorithms and one deep learning-based algorithm with a total of six algorithms. Traditional ML algorithms are Random Forest (RF), Support Vector Machine (SVM) with Linear kernel, SVM with Radial Basis Function (RBF) kernel, Naïve Bayes (NB), and Generalized Linear Model (GLM). The DL-based algorithm is Artificial Neural Network (ANN). For the evaluation purpose, we prepare a land cover ground truth (actual) dataset of the City of Melbourne, Victoria, Australia. 2. (2) We perform the category-wise analysis of the best-performing scheme (Sp) + (St) + (Ind) used in our work. Here, we also study the importance of variables in the feature combination along with the model interpretability for generalisability at the category level. 3. (3) We carry out the detailed robustness analysis of ML algorithms using varying training splits at the category level and overall performance level. 4. (4) We conduct pairwise comparisons between ML algorithms on performance measures using statistical analysis. This paper is organised into five sections. Section “Related works” briefly explains recent feature extraction methods that have been used in LULC classification. Section “Materials and methods” presents the study area in detail, the dataset, and the proposed method. Section “Results and discussion” analyses and discusses LULC classification and ML algorithms’ performance. Finally, section “Conclusion and future works” draws conclusions and presents recommendations. Contextual neighborhood information improves landcover classification by adding spatial relationships beyond the pixel itself, reducing ambiguity, and improving class separation. The evidence points to a hybrid segmentation procedure that “integrates contextual information with per-pixel classification” in a metropolitan area land cover project [N1-R1], and to a broader comparison showing that object-based classification can outperform pixel-based classification in overall accuracy [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3]. This matters because pixel-based classification uses only spectral information for each individual pixel, while neighborhood-based methods implicitly or explicitly model how neighboring pixels relate to one another [N3-R4].

The types of neighborhood information used in classification models are mostly spatial or contextual units that go beyond single pixels. The cited work on contextual landcover classification explicitly mentions “contextual information” as part of a hybrid segmentation approach [N1-R1], and the comparative pixel vs object-based study emphasizes object-based image analysis as a way to use information among units rather than only within pixels [N3-F2]. In practical terms, neighborhood modeling can take the form of object-oriented segmentation, spatial adjacency, texture features, or contextual scene relationships [N1-R1][N1-R3][N3-F2].

Neighborhood information helps distinguish landcover classes by reducing confusion caused by mixed pixels or spatially similar classes. The evidence suggests that spatial information can improve classification when integrated with textural and spectral imagery [N4-R1]. In a complex urban-rural landscape study, the authors specifically state that using spatial information during classification helps reduce heterogeneity and improve separation [N4-R1][N4-R4]. Object-based methods are useful in this regard because they capture relationships among neighboring regions rather than treating each pixel in isolation, which can resolve cases where a single pixel is ambiguous or belongs to a mixed-pixel class [N3-F2][N4-R4].

Performance metrics showing improvement from neighborhood modeling are mainly overall accuracy and classification accuracy differences. The pixel-based vs object-based comparison reports that object-based classification achieved higher overall accuracy than pixel-based classification in some studies [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3]. In one study, object-based image analysis produced a visually appealing generalized appearance of land cover classes, while pixel-based classifications used fewer variables and required less time to produce [N3-F2]. Another study on urban land cover mapping using pixel-based versus object-based fusion found that object-based methods had a statistically significant difference in classification accuracy across different machine learning algorithms [N3-F2]. These results support the claim that neighborhood modeling can improve classification performance, though the evidence does not uniformly show large absolute gains in every case [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3].

Overall, contextual neighborhood information improves landcover classification by leveraging spatial relationships among pixels or objects, reducing ambiguity, and improving separation between classes, especially in complex or mixed-pixel scenes. The strongest evidence is that object-based methods and contextual integration can produce higher overall accuracy and more visually coherent landcover maps than purely pixel-based approaches [N1-R1][N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-F2].

Texture features improve landcover classification by capturing spatial structure that pixel values alone cannot express. The evidence repeatedly links texture features to improved classification performance, especially when combined with spectral information. In a crop classification study, GLCM-based texture features outperformed grayscale images, achieving an overall accuracy margin of 13.65% [N2-R1][N2-F1]. Another study found that combining texture features with spectral features improved classification accuracy compared to using only spectral features [N5-R2]. This indicates that texture is particularly useful when classes are difficult to separate based on spectral values alone, because texture encodes spatial arrangement, intensity patterns, and local structure [N2-R3][N2-F1].

The most relevant texture features for landcover discrimination in the evidence are GLCM-derived features. The cited study explicitly uses contrast, homogeneity, dimensionality, angular second moment, energy, and correlation as texture features [N2-F1]. It also notes that larger kernel sizes in GLCM extraction improved classification results by 7.72% in overall accuracy compared to spectral-only classification [N2-F1]. A separate study on high-resolution remote sensing land use classification mentions “object GLCM texture features” as an effective method [N2-R2], while another source describes GLCM as one of the most used methods for satellite image texture measurements [N2-R5]. These references establish GLCM as a central texture feature class for landcover discrimination, especially in high-resolution or heterogeneous scenes [N2-R2][N2-R5][N2-F1].

Texture captures spatial structure that pixel values alone miss because it encodes how intensities or values are distributed across a region. The evidence states that texture features provide a quantitative way to describe “the visual characteristics of different surfaces and objects in remote sensing” [N2-R3]. In crop classification, texture features provided useful insights into color, its spatial arrangement, and intensities [N2-F1]. A textural approach for land cover classification is also described as significant because traditional texture models capture only patterns with discrete boundaries [N4-R5]. This means texture helps distinguish landcover classes by revealing patterns such as regularity, texture coarseness, spatial repetition, and local spatial coherence, which may not be visible from pixel values alone [N2-R3][N2-F1][N4-R5].

The trade-offs of using texture features include increased computational cost, feature dimensionality, and the risk of overfitting or overcomplicating the model. The evidence shows that pixel-based classifications can use fewer variables than object-based approaches [N3-F2]. In the GLCM crop study, the authors used multiple texture features and multiple classification algorithms, which suggests that texture can increase the number of input features and thus the complexity of the model [N2-F1]. While this can improve accuracy, it can also make the model harder to interpret and more sensitive to noise or overfitting, especially when the feature space becomes large [N2-F1][N3-F2]. The cited study also notes that texture information is often integrated with spectral and other geospatial features [N4-R1][N5-R2], which implies that texture is most useful when used in combination rather than as a standalone feature [N4-R1][N5-R2].

In short, texture features improve landcover classification by encoding spatial structure, especially through GLCM-derived measures like contrast, homogeneity, and energy. They help separate classes that are spectrally similar but spatially different, but they also introduce trade-offs such as increased complexity and potential overfitting [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R5][N2-F1][N4-R1][N5-R2].

## 4) How neighborhood, texture, and contextual features interact in landcover classification

Neighborhood, texture, and contextual features interact in landcover classification by complementing one another: neighborhood information captures local spatial relationships, texture captures structural and intensity patterns, and contextual/semantic information captures broader scene relationships. The evidence shows that object-based image analysis and contextual integration improve overall accuracy compared to pixel-based classification [N3-F2][N4-R1][N4-R4]. Texture features, especially GLCM-based features, improve classification when combined with spectral information [N2-R1][N2-F1][N5-R2]. Contextual and semantic information further enhance classification by leveraging object relationships and scene structure [N6-R3][N6-R4]. Together, these feature types help a model distinguish classes that are spectrally similar but spatially different [N2-F1][N4-R1][N6-R3].

Neighborhood and texture information complement each other by addressing different spatial scales. Neighborhood modeling, whether object-based or spatial adjacency-based, adds relationships among neighboring pixels or objects [N1-R1][N3-F2]. Texture features capture local spatial structure, such as contrast, homogeneity, and energy, which can reveal patterns that are not captured by single-pixel values alone [N2-R3][N2-F1]. In the GLCM crop study, larger kernel sizes improved classification results by 7.72% in overall accuracy, showing that texture can encode more detailed spatial structure than spectral features alone [N2-F1]. At the same time, object-based methods and contextual integration help resolve cases where a single pixel or small neighborhood is ambiguous [N3-F2][N4-R1]. This suggests that neighborhood and texture information work best when they are used together: texture captures fine-scale spatial patterns, while neighborhood/contextual modeling captures broader spatial coherence and object relationships [N2-F1][N3-F2][N4-R1].

Contextual information interacts with both neighborhood and texture features by providing higher-level scene structure. The evidence on semantic understanding and spatial context models shows that multi-object spatial context relationships can be used to improve scene understanding [N6-R3]. In a deep-learning review, semantic information is described as being captured through intermediate layers of CNNs [N6-F3]. Limitations and overfitting risks arise when combined features become too complex. The evidence notes that pixel-based classifications can use fewer variables than object-based approaches [N3-F2]. ## 5) Bottom-line synthesis

Incorporating contextual neighborhood information and texture features enhances pixel-based landcover classification in three main ways:

Texture captures spatial structure that pixel values alone miss because it encodes how intensities or values are distributed across a region. The evidence states that texture features provide a quantitative way to describe “the visual characteristics of different surfaces and objects in remote sensing” [N2-R3]. In crop classification, texture features provided useful insights into color, its spatial arrangement, and intensities [N2-F1]. A textural approach for land cover classification is also described as significant because traditional texture models capture only patterns with discrete boundaries [N4-R5]. This means texture helps distinguish landcover classes by revealing patterns such as regularity, texture coarseness, spatial repetition, and local spatial coherence, which may not be visible from pixel values alone [N2-R3][N2-F1][N4-R5].

The trade-offs of using texture features include increased computational cost, feature dimensionality, and the risk of overfitting or overcomplicating the model. The evidence shows that pixel-based classifications can use fewer variables than object-based approaches [N3-F2]. In the GLCM crop study, the authors used multiple texture features and multiple classification algorithms, which suggests that texture can increase the number of input features and thus the complexity of the model [N2-F1]. While this can improve accuracy, it can also make the model harder to interpret and more sensitive to noise or overfitting, especially when the feature space becomes large [N2-F1][N3-F2]. The cited study also notes that texture information is often integrated with spectral and other geospatial features [N4-R1][N5-R2], which implies that texture is most useful when used in combination rather than as a standalone feature [N4-R1][N5-R2].

## 3) How contextual and semantic information enhance landcover classification

Contextual and semantic information improve landcover classification by leveraging scene context and object relationships rather than relying solely on local pixel values. The evidence points to a bottom-up scene understanding framework based on a multi-object spatial context relationship model (MOSCRF) [N6-R3]. It also cites a study on contextual information in landcover classification and a review of deep-learning-based land use/land cover classification that emphasizes the importance of contextual and semantic information [N6-R1][N6-R4]. Together, these sources support the idea that classification benefits when the model uses relationships among objects, spatial context, and semantic structure rather than just isolated spectral measurements [N6-R3][N6-R1][N6-R4].

The kind of scene context or semantic relationships used includes spatial context, object relationships, and semantic associations. The MOSCRF paper explicitly uses a multi-object spatial context relationship model, indicating that context is modeled through interactions among objects [N6-R3]. Another source notes that deep-learning-based methods can capture “highly discriminating semantic information through its intermediate layers” [N6-F3], which aligns with the broader idea that semantic relationships help the model understand the meaning of objects in a scene [N6-R4][N6-R5]. The evidence also suggests that contextual information can be derived from spatial relationships and object-oriented analysis, as object-based methods are part of the broader image analysis approaches used in land cover classification [N3-F2][N6-R4].

Contextual information helps resolve ambiguous or mixed-pixel cases by reducing uncertainty through scene-level relationships. The evidence states that object-based image analysis can produce a visually appealing generalized appearance of land cover classes [N3-F2]. In a complex urban-rural landscape study, the authors argue that using spatial information during classification helps reduce heterogeneity and improve separation [N4-R1][N4-R4]. This implies that when a pixel is ambiguous or belongs to a mixed-pixel class, the surrounding context can clarify its likely class membership by considering how neighboring regions relate to one another [N4-R1][N4-R4]. The study also notes that auxiliary datasets can improve object-based LULC classification accuracy when compared to using only spectral and textural features [N4-R2], further supporting the role of contextual and external information in resolving ambiguity [N4-R2].

Performance gains from contextual modeling are indicated by improved overall accuracy and better classification coherence. The comparative pixel vs object-based study reports that object-based classification can outperform pixel-based classification in overall accuracy [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3]. In the same source, object-based image analysis produced a more visually adequate depiction of wetland, riparian, and crop land cover types [N3-F2]. The contextual landcover study also states that using spatial information during classification can improve results [N4-R1]. Taken together, the evidence supports the conclusion that contextual modeling leads to better separation, more accurate classification, and more interpretable maps, especially in complex scenes [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3][N4-R1][N6-R3].

## 4) How neighborhood, texture, and contextual features interact in landcover classification

Neighborhood, texture, and contextual features interact in landcover classification by complementing one another: neighborhood information captures local spatial relationships, texture captures structural and intensity patterns, and contextual/semantic information captures broader scene relationships. The evidence shows that object-based image analysis and contextual integration improve overall accuracy compared to pixel-based classification [N3-F2][N4-R1][N4-R4]. Texture features, especially GLCM-based features, improve classification when combined with spectral information [N2-R1][N2-F1][N5-R2]. Contextual and semantic information further enhance classification by leveraging object relationships and scene structure [N6-R3][N6-R4]. Together, these feature types help a model distinguish classes that are spectrally similar but spatially different [N2-F1][N4-R1][N6-R3].

Neighborhood and texture information complement each other by addressing different spatial scales. Neighborhood modeling, whether object-based or spatial adjacency-based, adds relationships among neighboring pixels or objects [N1-R1][N3-F2]. Texture features capture local spatial structure, such as contrast, homogeneity, and energy, which can reveal patterns that are not captured by single-pixel values alone [N2-R3][N2-F1]. In the GLCM crop study, larger kernel sizes improved classification results by 7.72% in overall accuracy, showing that texture can encode more detailed spatial structure than spectral features alone [N2-F1]. At the same time, object-based methods and contextual integration help resolve cases where a single pixel or small neighborhood is ambiguous [N3-F2][N4-R1]. This suggests that neighborhood and texture information work best when they are used together: texture captures fine-scale spatial patterns, while neighborhood/contextual modeling captures broader spatial coherence and object relationships [N2-F1][N3-F2][N4-R1].

Contextual information interacts with both neighborhood and texture features by providing higher-level scene structure. The evidence on semantic understanding and spatial context models shows that multi-object spatial context relationships can be used to improve scene understanding [N6-R3]. In a deep-learning review, semantic information is described as being captured through intermediate layers of CNNs [N6-F3]. This means that contextual information can refine the interpretation of local features: a pixel or texture pattern may be ambiguous on its own, but becomes more meaningful when the model also knows where it is located in the scene and what other objects or regions are nearby [N6-R3][N6-R4]. The cited study on contextual landcover classification also emphasizes that spatial information can improve classification when integrated with textural and spectral imagery [N4-R1]. This indicates that contextual modeling can act as a bridge between local features and scene-level understanding, reducing errors caused by noise, mixed pixels, or ambiguous spatial arrangements [N4-R1][N6-R3].

Limitations and overfitting risks arise when combined features become too complex. The evidence notes that pixel-based classifications can use fewer variables than object-based approaches [N3-F2]. In the GLCM crop study, using multiple texture features and multiple classification algorithms suggests that adding texture can increase feature dimensionality and model complexity [N2-F1]. Object-based methods also produce more variables and more visually generalized results, which can sometimes obscure fine-scale details [N3-F2]. Additionally, the evidence on deep learning emphasizes that DL-based methods can be less interpretable and explainable, which is a concern when combining many features [N5-F3]. These trade-offs imply that while neighborhood, texture, and contextual features can improve accuracy, they also require careful selection, regularization, and validation to avoid overfitting, computational overload, or loss of interpretability [N3-F2][N2-F1][N5-F3].

## 5) Bottom-line synthesis

Incorporating contextual neighborhood information and texture features enhances pixel-based landcover classification in three main ways:

1. **Neighborhood information** adds spatial relationships beyond the pixel, reducing ambiguity and improving class separation, especially in complex or mixed-pixel scenes [N1-R1][N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3][N4-R1][N4-R4].
2. **Texture features** capture spatial structure and local intensity patterns that pixel values alone miss, improving discrimination when classes are spectrally similar but spatially different [N2-R1][N2-F1][N5-R2][N2-R3][N2-R5][N4-R5].
3. **Contextual and semantic information** provide higher-level scene relationships and object associations, helping resolve ambiguous cases and improving overall classification coherence and accuracy [N6-R3][N6-R1][N6-R4][N3-F2][N4-R1][N4-R4].

Taken together, these features complement one another: neighborhood and texture address local spatial structure, while contextual information provides broader scene-level coherence. However, they also introduce trade-offs such as increased complexity, feature dimensionality, and potential overfitting [N2-F1][N3-F2][N5-F3]. Overall, the evidence supports the conclusion that contextual neighborhood and texture features can significantly enhance pixel-based landcover classification by making the model more robust to ambiguity and more capable of distinguishing spectrally similar classes [N1-R1][N2-R1][N3-R1][N4-R1][N5-R2][N6-R3].
